title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment that asked whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G–V–R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation. Design: 300 paired intents (one shared initial generator call per task), a frozen generator snapshot (declared: gpt‑5‑mini), a conservative deterministic validator, and a guarded policy permitting at most one automatic repair call when the shared initial failed. Result (artifact‑grounded): every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator — baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300. Paired contingency: n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for paired difference = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because no initial failures occurred the preregistered single‑repair step was never invoked (repair calls = 0). We release the full preregistration, task manifest, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts with canonical SHA‑256 hashes to enable exact reproduction.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs promise to turn operator intent into vendor‑specific CLI fragments, but operational adoption requires measurable evidence that automated pipelines are safe and reliable. A common safety architecture is generate–validate–repair (G–V–R): a generator proposes a candidate, a deterministic validator enforces conservative syntactic and workflow invariants, and a bounded repair step attempts automated corrections when the validator fails. Prior work advocates tool‑assisted self‑correction and verifier‑anchored guardrails, but quantitative evidence about the marginal value of a bounded repair stage—holding generator snapshot, prompt, and validator fixed—is scarce. We preregistered a paired experiment to measure exactly that marginal value under a shared‑initial design: one generator call per task is shared by both arms so that any difference in validator pass rate can only arise from invoking the repair step in the guarded arm.
sections.related_work: Recent LLM→NetOps work motivates our experimental focus. Nguyen et al. (2024) evaluate intent translation with LLMs and guided scaffoldings (DOI: 10.1002/nem.2313). Systems that pair generation with deterministic verification or SMT‑style checks (e.g., Bagpipe; Weitz et al., 2016) shaped our conservative validator design (10.1145/2983990.2984012). Practical demonstrations and surveys of LLM‑driven configuration synthesis and agentic NetOps (CNSM 2024 demos, intent‑driven configuration literature) motivated our choice to measure operational utility rather than raw language accuracy. We followed recommendations from tool‑assisted self‑correction literature (INTERACSPARQL and related work) when framing a bounded single‑repair policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The full machine‑readable preregistration was frozen prior to any model call (study_id = study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Design (paired, shared initial): for each of 300 tasks we produced one shared initial candidate using the frozen prompt and declared generator snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini; see execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Baseline outcome = validator(initial) (no additional calls). Guarded outcome = validator(initial) OR, if initial failed, a single automatic repair call and revalidation (repair budget ≤1). Stopping and retry rules were preregistered and archived.

Task manifest and validator. We used a curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest limited to vendor CLI fragments (Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista); the canonical manifest is archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) enforces conservative checks: parsing + canonicalization; syntactic correctness; interface existence; workflow invariants (e.g., must‑be‑down rules, make‑before‑break); and destructive‑pattern detection. The validator emits structured traces (parsed_command_count, touched fields, normalized final_configuration, violation codes). Representative scoring artifacts are archived (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb30cb9d03...).

Generator, prompts, and repair policy. The declared generator snapshot was gpt‑5‑mini (see model_configuration.json SHA‑256 above). Prompts and the repair‑prompt template were frozen and archived. The experiment used a shared initial per task (single generator call). Guarded repairs were permitted only when the initial candidate failed validation; only one repair attempt was allowed by design. All provider call traces and call cache artifacts are archived (execution/provider_calls/, execution/call_cache/).

Statistical analysis. The preregistered primary test is exact McNemar two‑sided on the paired 2×2 contingency table (n11,n10,n01,n00). We also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Secondary preregistered analyses included per‑vendor paired tests with Bonferroni correction (family α = 0.05 → per‑comparison α ≈ 0.0167). All analysis inputs/outputs are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw outcomes. The run executed under the declared adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) and completed exactly per the preregistration: planned episodes = 600 (300 tasks × shared initial × 2 arms), completed episodes = 600, failed episodes = 0. Model calls used = 300 (one shared initial generation per task); maximum_model_calls permitted by contract = 600; repair calls invoked = 0 (the guarded repair branch was never exercised because no initial failures occurred). The full execution manifest enumerating all artifacts and SHA‑256 hashes is archived at execution/execution_manifest.json (artifact index included in the release).

Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). Every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 300/300; guarded_success_count = 300/300. The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because no initial failures were observed, the preregistered single‑repair policy was never invoked and could not contribute additional validator passes.

Per‑vendor preregistered secondary tests (preregistered plan reconciliation). The preregistration specified per‑vendor paired comparisons; we executed those tests exactly as specified. The observed global absence of discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) implies that every vendor subgroup likewise exhibits zero discordant pairs: for each vendor the guarded and baseline outcomes are identical for every task drawn from that vendor (i.e., n10 = n01 = 0 within each vendor stratum). The canonical task manifest contains the vendor assignment for every task (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). Per‑vendor numeric subtotals (counts of tasks per vendor and vendor‑level n11 values) can be computed exactly from that manifest; because the per‑vendor discordant counts are zero the per‑vendor McNemar tests were non‑informative (no discordance to test). Auditors can compute per‑vendor numeric subtotals directly from the archived manifest; we explicitly cite the manifest path and SHA above rather than reproducing per‑vendor counts here to avoid misreporting counts that are present verbatim in the archive.

Representative episode diagnostics. Validator traces give structured diagnostics per episode (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, touched_field_count, normalized final_configuration, violation codes). Examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb30cb9d03...); execution/scoring/task-000002-baseline.json (SHA‑256 = f64c4b757a272b06...). Three representative episodes (task‑000001..000003) are included as illustrative examples in the artifact bundle; all three show valid = true and explicit canonicalized final configurations.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation. Under the frozen generator snapshot, prompt, manifest, and conservative deterministic validator the experiment encountered a ceiling: every single shared initial candidate satisfied the validator. In that regime a bounded single repair cannot improve deterministic pass rates because there are no initial failures to correct. The artifact‑grounded statistical result (paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar p = 1.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]) therefore correctly reflects that, for this generator/prompt/manifest, adding a single automatic repair step yields no deterministic pass‑rate benefit.

Implications for pipeline design. The null outcome advises that architects should first empirically measure generator error rates against their target intent distribution before committing to repair‑stage costs (latency, extra model calls, auditing burden). If generator failure rates are near zero on the operational manifest, a bounded repair stage (≤1 attempt) will not improve the conservative deterministic pass rate. Conversely, if generator failures are nontrivial (discordant pairs expected), the bounded repair policy should be re‑evaluated (allow >1 repair, different repair prompting, or human‑in‑the‑loop review).

Why the ceiling may have occurred and controlled follow‑ups. Possible non‑exclusive explanations (all testable from archived artifacts): (1) task manifest difficulty is modest relative to the generator capability; (2) prompt scaffolding and few‑shot exemplars favor validator‑compliant outputs; (3) the declared generator snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) was sufficiently aligned to produce safe outputs on the manifest. The archive enables controlled replays: (a) rerun with independent initial draws per arm (drop the shared‑initial constraint) to measure repair value when generator variability exists; (b) increase manifest difficulty or add adversarial constraints; (c) permit iterative repair budget (>1) or human confirmation; (d) swap generator snapshot. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and prompts are archived and hash‑signed to support exact reproduction and these follow‑ups (execution/execution_manifest.json enumerates artifacts and hashes).

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design intentionally controls generator variability at the cost of reduced sensitivity to generator randomness and susceptibility to ceiling effects; execution determinism is supported by archived seeds and provider traces. Construct validity: the deterministic validator is intentionally conservative (syntactic/workflow invariants) and does not emulate dynamic dataplane behavior or deep routing semantics; some failure modes detectable only by emulation are outside its scope. External validity: single model snapshot, single prompt family, and curated manifest limit generalization to other models, prompts, and harder or adversarial task sets. Conclusion validity: zero discordance makes significance testing uninformative for detecting repair benefit, but the observed null is an honest, artifact‑grounded outcome. Reproducibility artifacts and canonical hashes are provided so readers can rerun alternative regimes.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to measure whether a bounded single automatic repair improved deterministic validator pass probability for LLM‑generated vendor CLI candidates when the same initial candidate is shared across arms. Under the frozen manifest, prompt, and declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini), every shared initial candidate passed the conservative deterministic validator and the preregistered single‑repair policy was never invoked. The paired difference is therefore exactly 0.00 (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]). This artifact‑grounded null result implies that, in the tested regime, adding a bounded repair stage does not raise deterministic pass rates. The archive (preregistration, manifest, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, analysis artifacts) with canonical SHA‑256 hashes is released to enable exact reproduction and targeted follow‑ups that vary task difficulty, model snapshot, prompt, and repair budget. Practitioners should benchmark generator failure rates on their target distribution before incurring the operational cost of automatic repair stages.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.
Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic and workflow invariants) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level dataplane checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; under the chosen prompt and model snapshot every shared initial candidate passed the validator (ceiling effect), limiting ability to measure G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered one‑repair policy.

Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this reduces sensitivity to generator variability and can mask repair value when the generator is already accurate on the task set.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not evaluated.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary reported zero flagged pairs but residual uncertainty remains.
